extracted.intended_audience: Authors submitting to F1000Research who are asked/suggesting peer reviewers
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for authors on identifying and suggesting suitable peer reviewers for articles published on F1000Research under its open, post-publication peer review model. Covers reviewer eligibility criteria, conflicts of interest, diversity requirements, tools and methods for finding reviewers, and dos/don'ts for suggesting reviewers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Peer review model — Identity transparency
rubrics_metrics.description: Identity transparency: All identities visible. Reviewer interacts with: Editor, other reviewers, authors. Review information published: Review reports, submitted manuscript, reviewer identities. Post publication commenting: Open.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This summarises F1000Research's open and transparent peer review model per NISO standard terminology — reviewers' identities and review reports are published alongside the article; understanding this model is relevant when suggesting reviewers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial team manages reviewer invitations
rubrics_metrics.description: The peer review process is managed by the editorial team, who identify and invite appropriate experts from relevant fields. Authors may suggest reviewers but the editorial team check they meet criteria before inviting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The editorial team may also suggest suitable reviewers when required and act as the intermediary between authors and reviewers. If you disagree with a rejection of a suggested reviewer, contact the Editorial Team to discuss options.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reviewer Finder Tool / algorithm use
rubrics_metrics.description: F1000Research provides a reviewer finding algorithm which scans the article and reference list to identify researchers who may be suitable to review the article. Authors can suggest reviewers from this automatically generated list or suggest their own.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors must use their own judgement to determine if suggested reviewers from the algorithm have the appropriate expertise. The tool is accessible via 'Suggest Reviewers' in My Research; it provides a ranked list based on leading authors of related published studies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Qualified — typical doctorate requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviewers should typically hold a doctorate (PhD/MD/MBBS or equivalent). Exceptions will be made for scholarly disciplines where doctorates are not necessary (e.g. Education, Library Science), or when an individual has a demonstrable public record of expertise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a suggested reviewer is rejected due to lack of qualifications, the editorial team will, if possible, suggest that their Principal Investigator/Supervisor is invited instead, and the original person could then take the role of co-reviewer.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expert — publication record requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviewers should have published at least three articles as lead author in a relevant topic, with at least one article having been published in the last five years.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In fields where expertise is not typically measured by publication record, or where demonstrated expertise exists in other ways, authors should provide an explanation of the suggested reviewer's suitability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Impartiality / conflict of interest restrictions
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviewers should not have any competing interests that can bias their assessment: they should not be close collaborators or personally associated with authors. For example, a reviewer should not have co-authored with any of the lead authors in the three years preceding publication of Version 1, have co-authored with any of the lead authors since the publication of Version 1, currently work at the same institution as the authors, or be a close collaborator with an author.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exceptions may be considered in small/specialized fields; authors should contact the Editorial Team to discuss cases where non-independent reviewers are unavoidable. Note also consortia publications exceptions (e.g., when researchers have published together on findings from a large consortia).

rubrics_metrics.name: Institutional and geographic diversity requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: For any given article, reviewers are required to be from different institutions. The editorial team also strongly encourages geographically-diverse reviewers to gain an international perspective.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This does not apply to large, multi-site institutions (e.g., Max-Planck Institutes, University of California). If multiple suggestions are from the same country, the editorial team can typically invite only one at a time — providing geographically diverse candidates can prevent review delays.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statistics expertise for complex analyses
rubrics_metrics.description: If your study includes complex statistical analysis or new statistical methods, ensure that at least one of your initial reviewer suggestions has a proven track record as a statistics expert.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be aware the editorial team may ask you to suggest additional statistics experts as the peer review process progresses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do — suggest experts in the relevant subject area
rubrics_metrics.description: Make sure suggested reviewers are experts in the relevant subject area. F1000Research will only invite reviewers who have expertise in the field of research covered by the article.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Selecting reviewers with close subject matter expertise ensures thorough peer review and increases the likelihood they will agree to provide a report.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do — ensure reviewers are from separate institutions and globally spread
rubrics_metrics.description: Try and ensure a global spread of reviewers. For any given article, reviewers must come from separate institutions and should not be affiliated with the authors' institutions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Geographically-diverse reviewers are encouraged to ensure international perspectives are represented and to avoid delays caused by multiple suggested reviewers from the same country.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do — verify algorithm-suggested reviewers before approving
rubrics_metrics.description: Ensure reviewers from the algorithm are suitable before approving them. The Reviewer Finder Tool automatically provides a list of researchers who have published related articles, but authors must use their own judgement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors can access the tool via the 'Suggest Reviewers' link in My Research. The tool is a starting point — manual checking of expertise, conflicts, and suitability is required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do — discuss reviewer suggestions with co-authors and contact editorial team if needed
rubrics_metrics.description: Discuss suggested reviewers with your co-authors; only the submitting author can provide suggestions, but the editorial team is willing to change the submitting author if needed. Contact the editorial team if you have questions or if you believe a rejected reviewer is appropriate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors can request editorial help to explore options if a suggested reviewer is rejected or if they are unsure about criteria applicability in their field.

rubrics_metrics.name: Don't — suggest recent close collaborators or same-institution reviewers
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not suggest reviewers who have recently closely collaborated with you or your co-authors. A reviewer should not be based at the same institution as any author, be a close collaborator, or have co-authored with any of the lead authors for three years before the publication of the article.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is considered a potential conflict of interest. Exceptions exist for large consortia; contact the editorial team for guidance in special cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Don't — suggest reviewers lacking appropriate expertise
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not suggest reviewers who do not have the right expertise. The editorial team will not invite reviewers who do not appear to have appropriate expertise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Suggesting inappropriate reviewers can cause significant delays to the peer review process.

rubrics_metrics.name: Don't — contact reviewers directly about the peer review
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors should not approach reviewers about the peer review process independently. Contacting reviewers directly has the potential to influence and invalidate their review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The editorial team acts as intermediary; directly contacting reviewers could dissuade them from reviewing or be considered coercion. If evidence of coercion is found, F1000Research will investigate and take appropriate action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical methods for finding potential reviewers
rubrics_metrics.description: Methods include: using authors of references cited in your article; searching databases (Google Scholar, PubMed, Web of Science, Scopus or subject-specific databases) for recent articles with specific keywords; searching prominent lab websites; using Journal/Author Name Estimator and similar tools.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These methods help identify authors currently working in the same field. Note some indexing services (Web of Science, Scopus) may be subscription-based and not available at all institutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Handling of suggested reviewers rejected for lack of qualifications
rubrics_metrics.description: If a reviewer suggestion is rejected due to lack of qualifications, the editorial team will, if possible, suggest the Principal Investigator/Supervisor is invited instead, and the original person could then take the role of co-reviewer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This provides a pathway for less-qualified but knowledgeable junior researchers to contribute as co-reviewers under the supervision of a qualified invited reviewer.
